item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports contrastive alignment between item text and sequential behavior, but the closest results rely on pretrained language models. [CLA-Rec (ICDM 2024)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10884256/) aligns LLM-derived description embeddings with collaborative representations, then models sequences with a Transformer. [CALRec (RecSys 2024)](https://research.google/pubs/calrec-contrastive-alignment-of-generative-llms-for-sequential-recommendation/) combines recommendation and contrastive objectives using pretrained PaLM-2. [ADRec (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0950705125003375) studies sequence–target alignment with decoupled contrastive learning and expanded negatives. These provide auxiliary-objective ideas, not verified evidence for a text encoder trained from scratch inside NextItNet. No exact match satisfying all those constraints was identified in the retrieved sources.\n\nA plausible experiment, inferred from these approaches: retain NextItNet’s causal convolutions; jointly train a small token-embedding encoder over titles/descriptions; integrate its output into each item representation; add a lightly weighted item-ID–text alignment loss alongside next-item prediction. Use the same item’s ID and text as the positive pair, rather than declaring broadly related products interchangeable. Textually similar but distinct items could supply harder negatives, although this remains an unverified hypothesis. [CaDiRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.09369) cautions that semantic distortions from augmentation can impair sequential learning, supporting conservative auxiliary supervision. Use only available text, one jointly trained network and one checkpoint per category; assess whether alignment improves exact-item discrimination through the fixed validation HR@10 benchmark."}
